newsitem.title: INDIA: India basks in glow of bold budget plan.
newsitem.headline: India basks in glow of bold budget plan.

text.p: The Indian government, riding a wave of enthusiasm over an ambitious new budget plan, on Saturday predicted robust economic growth and declining inflation over the next year.
The Finance Ministry said gross domestic product (GDP), adjusted for inflation, would grow by seven percent or more in the 1997/98 fiscal year beginning on April 1.
That would be up from a projected 6.8 percent in the current year and yield an average annual growth rate of seven percent over four years -- unprecedented in independent India.
Inflation, considered by some to be the Achilles' heel of the economy, will come down over the next year, Shankar Acharya, the ministry's chief economic adviser, told a news conference.
"Our view is that we will see real GDP growth of seven percent-plus and we will see perhaps inflation at most for the average of the year at 6.5 to 7.0 percent," Acharya said.
The year-on-year inflation rate measured by the wholesale price index rose to 7.99 percent in the week ending February 8.

Acharya was speaking a day after Finance Minister P. Chidambaram unveiled a bold, business-friendly budget for the 1997/98 year that slashed taxes and tariffs and took the six-year-old reform of the economy forward in a big leap.
The government's economic tsars said the budget would stimulate economic growth while soaking up red ink.

Propelled higher by corporate tax cuts and investor-friendly market reforms in the budget, the main share price index on the Bombay Stock Exchange's benchmark surged 5.56 percent on Saturday after jumping 5.13 percent on Friday.
"Mr Chidambaram's second budget may achieve the near miracle of being welcomed by all sections of society," the Hindustan Times newspaper said.
"The finance minister has proved that it is possible to please all," stock brokers James Capal B&K said.
Investors hailed a cut in domestic corporate tax rates to 35 percent from 40 percent, as well as the scrapping of a corporate tax surcharge and a tax on income from dividends.
Taxpayers were given across-the-board cuts in personal income tax rates, while more money was committed to anti-poverty and welfare programmes.
Revenue Secretary N.K. Singh said the government would haul in more money despite the cut in tax rates.

Corporations would pay more tax because profits would swell, while a new compliance scheme to lure owners of luxury items like houses, cars and telephones into the tax net would raise personal income tax revenues, he predicted.
Acharya said the prices of some goods might rise due to increases in excise rates, but there would be no upward pressure on overall prices.
"We are very confident that you will see a softening of inflationary pressure because of this budget," Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia said.

Ahluwalia, the highest ranking civil servant in the Finance Ministry, said a plan to sell off 48 billion rupees' worth ($1.3 billion) of shares in state-controlled firms was likely to succeed because of a more bullish attitude among investors.

The government had planned to unload 50 billion rupees' worth in 1996/97, but because of lacklustre capital markets has yet to sell a single share with less than a month left in the fiscal year. ($1 = 35.90 rupees)
